title: Only obviously simple behavior is reducible; nearly all else is irreducible

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Only obviously simple behavior is reducible; nearly all else is irreducible

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Behavior that is obviously simple, such as repetitive or nested behavior, is always computationally reducible, while in practically all other cases behavior is computationally irreducible.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: If the behavior of a system is obviously simple—and is say either repetitive or nested—then it will always be computationally reducible. But it follows from the Principle of Computational Equivalence that in practically all other cases it will be computationally irreducible.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Computational Irreducibility” (from p. 737), p. 741. Scope: all systems, especially simple programs

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-14: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.43

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Finite program catalogs can test restricted, formalized versions and find counterexamples. They cannot establish a prevalence claim over all systems, and the categories require substantial interpretation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Specify system classes, formal measures of repetitive, nested, and reducible behavior, then classify each system using predictor runtimes or proofs. Reducible non-simple cases or irreducible repetitive cases would refute the corresponding universal component.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Observed complexity does not prove irreducibility.

Available enumerations cover only selected program families.

"Obviously simple" and "practically all" lack fixed thresholds.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Repetitive and nested elementary rules have known shortcuts that a public simulator can check against direct evolution, so the first clause is testable inside that class. The second clause quantifies over practically all remaining behavior, including natural systems, and a missed formula is weak evidence of irreducibility. Existing enumerations therefore probe a restricted proxy.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Classify small cellular automata as repetitive, nested, or neither, and check whether the first two classes have shortcuts while the others lack any procedure shorter than direct evolution. A nested rule with no shortcut, or a complex-looking rule with a large shortcut, would count against the corresponding clause.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Practically all and obviously simple are not tied to a measure over systems.

Elementary-rule enumerations cover a small slice of the stated scope.

Failure to find a shortcut leaves open whether a shortcut exists.
